subject: Estimating multiple independent series with a shared variance parameter

messages.author: c831d1b5d046d2a7
messages.subject: Estimating multiple independent series with a shared variance parameter
parts:
I'm trying to estimate roughly 200 stationary and independent AR(1) time series with measurement error over 8 time steps. Because there are so few observations per series, I wanted to pool the variance term over all of the observations, but the model I've coded up is converging very slowly: Effective sample size for the shared variance parameter was only 2 after 1000 iterations on four chains, roughly an hour's worth of computation after parallelization. 

I've attached the code for simulating a dataset and the STAN code, does anybody have any suggestions for speeding it up? 


data {
    int<lower=0> num_series; // Number of series
int<lower=0> num_periods; // Number of time periods
    int<lower=0> num_obs; // Number of observations
    real y[num_obs]; // Observed data
    int<lower=0> sample_size[num_obs]; // Sample Size of observation
    int<lower=0> time_period[num_obs]; // Time of observation
    int<lower=0> series_id[num_obs]; // subgroup of obs
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma_series; 
    real z[num_series,num_periods];
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;
  }
transformed parameters {
  real y_sigma[num_obs] ;
  real y_mean[num_obs] ;
  
for(i in 1:num_obs)
    y_mean[i]<-z[series_id[i],time_period[i]]  ;

  for(j in 1:num_obs)
    y_sigma[j] <- sigma_y/sqrt(sample_size[j]);
  

 
}
  model {
 

 
for(i in 1:num_series) 
      z[i,1]~normal(0,.05);
for(i in 1:num_series) 
for(t in 2:num_periods)
      z[i,t]~normal(z[i,t-1],sigma_series);     

   sigma_series~uniform(0,.01);
 
    y ~ normal(y_mean, y_sigma ) ;
    
 
    sigma_y~uniform(0,1);
 
 
  }

messages.author: 9dd9ea947d797759
messages.subject: Re: Estimating multiple independent series with a shared variance parameter
parts:
I have a related problem: see this thread for some suggestions:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/UykETq-tL64

(n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0). I have fewer time series (4 in the test case posted here, around 20 in the full data set) and more time steps (up to about 20), the time series are multivariate, and when we have observations, there are replicates.

For a univariate case, you can probably speed up by using tail instead of a loop. See pages 59-60 in the stan manual. For the univariate case I tried with just one series:

   //for (t in 2:T) {
       // z[t] ~ normal(mu + z[t - 1]*b, Sigma);
    //}
    tail(z, T-1) ~ normal(mu + head(z,T-1)*b, Sigma);

Can that be adapted to multiple series? It might be a bit harder. For multivariate series, I asked about it in this thread:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/W9Jp08YtYrk

There are some helpful suggestions there, which I didn't yet figure out how to implement.

You can probably also vectorize the observation model. For the case I tried (Poisson observation error, one time series) this made a big difference (you can do normal in a similar way):

    //// Observation model
    //for (t in 1:T) {
    //    x[t] ~ poisson(exp(z[t]));
    //}
    x ~poisson(exp(z));

Might also be worth checking trace plots of lp__. In my multivariate case, there's something that we didn't yet figure out, that's causing lp__ to stick at -Inf at some iteration. If this happens not long after the end of the warmup period, the effective sample size will be very small.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating multiple independent series with a shared variance parameter
parts:
The problem in your model is that you have this:

> real<lower=0> sigma_series;
...
> sigma_series~uniform(0,.01);


The declared constraints on a variable (here (0,inf)) should match
its support in the model (here (0,0.01)). You need to declare
sigma_series as

real<lower=0,upper=0.01> sigma_series;

at which point the uniform(0,0.01) is redundant (though doesn't
hurt much as Stan can figure out at compile time that everything
other than size checks on sigma_series are redundant.

Are you sure the right answer is in that range and not butting
up against a boundary? We'd usually recommend an unconstrained
sigma_series and a softer constraint, say

sigma_series ~ cauchy(0,0.005);

Same issue with sigma.

I'm not sure why you're dividing by sqrt of sample size
for the std devs in the model, but if you need to do it,
I'd recommend computing an inverse sqrt size vector in transformed
data and then multiplying that by sigma. You should probably move
the transformed parameters to local variables in the model --- I
don't see any reason to save them, which is what declaring them
as transformed parameters does.

> for(i in 1:num_series)
> z[i,1]~normal(0,.05);
> for(i in 1:num_series)
> for(t in 2:num_periods)
z[i,t]~normal(z[i,t-1],sigma_series);

This can be sped up considerably by rewriting as:

col(z,i) ~ normal(0, 0.05);
for (i in 1:num_series)
head(z[i],num_periods-1) ~ normal(tail(z[i],num_periods-1), sigma_series);

It's most efficient here if z is declared as an
array of vectors, because then there's no copying or
non-local memory required to compute z[i].

- Bob

> On Jan 6, 2015, at 3:21 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> For a univariate case, you can probably speed up by using tail instead of a loop. See pages 59-60 in the stan manual. For the univariate case I tried with just one series:
>
> //for (t in 2:T) {
> // z[t] ~ normal(mu + z[t - 1]*b, Sigma);
> //}
> tail(z, T-1) ~ normal(mu + head(z,T-1)*b, Sigma);
Exactly!
> Can that be adapted to multiple series? It might be a bit harder.

No problem --- see my response.

> ...

>
> //// Observation model
> //for (t in 1:T) {
> // x[t] ~ poisson(exp(z[t]));
> //}
> x ~poisson(exp(z));

You don't ever want to do this. We have a built-in Poisson on
the log scale, so you're much better of arithmetically and speedwise
with:

x ~ poisson_log(z);

> Might also be worth checking trace plots of lp__. In my multivariate case, there's something that we didn't yet figure out, that's causing lp__ to stick at -Inf at some iteration. If this happens not long after the end of the warmup period, the effective sample size will be very small.

Yup --- that shouldn't be happening and we still don't know
what's causing it.

- Bob
